name: Diabetic Foot Infection

likely: Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — especially in chronic or previously treated wounds
possible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (if wound exposed to water/soaking)
Anaerobes (if deep, necrotic, or malodorous wound)
pathogens.why: Mild superficial diabetic foot infections are usually monomicrobial with gram-positive cocci, while deeper, chronic, or previously treated wounds become polymicrobial, incorporating gram-negatives and anaerobes — empiric spectrum should match wound chronicity and depth.

investigations.test: Deep tissue/bone culture (avoid superficial swab alone)
investigations.why: Superficial swabs poorly correlate with the true infecting organism; deep culture better guides targeted therapy.
Screens for osteomyelitis and gas in soft tissue.

investigations.test: MRI (if osteomyelitis suspected and X-ray inconclusive)
investigations.why: More sensitive for early osteomyelitis than plain films.
Poor glycemic control impairs healing and infection clearance; relevant to overall management.
Peripheral arterial disease impairs healing and antibiotic delivery to tissue — relevant to overall treatment plan and need for revascularization.

reason: meets criteria for diabetic foot infection requiring antibiotics.
Suspected osteomyelitis requires imaging and likely prolonged therapy in conjunction with surgical/orthopedic input.
Severity (mild/moderate/severe per IDSA/IWGDF criteria) should guide route and spectrum.

clinicalPearls: A wound that probes to bone (rock-hard, gritty base without intervening soft tissue) strongly predicts underlying osteomyelitis; the probe-to-bone test has a positive predictive value of ~90% in high-pretest-probability populations (p.1112).

In a hospitalized diabetic patient with a chronic deep foot ulcer, the pretest probability of osteomyelitis is high (~65%), so a positive probe-to-bone test can often establish the diagnosis clinically without imaging (p.91, 1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test lowers the likelihood of osteomyelitis (likelihood ratio ~0.2) (p.92).

An infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis; superficial swab cultures recover multiple organisms of uncertain significance and correlate poorly with bone biopsy (only ~24% concordance in one study) (p.1111-1112, 3271-3272).
Culture-pathogen concordance between deep samples and bone is best for S. aureus (40-50%) and poorest for coagulase-negative staphylococci, anaerobes, and gram-negative bacilli (p.1112).
About 34% of people with diabetes develop a foot ulcer in their lifetime; among those with an ulcer, ~5% per year progress to foot osteomyelitis (p.1111).
Gas gangrene-like findings may occur in a diabetic foot wound even in the absence of clostridial infection (p.3272).
harrison.pathophysiology: Diabetic foot infection arises from the interaction of peripheral sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathy with abnormal foot biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and impaired wound healing. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain sensation, allowing unrecognized repetitive or major trauma; impaired proprioception causes abnormal weight-bearing and callus/ulcer formation. Motor and sensory neuropathy produce structural deformities (hammer/claw toe, prominent metatarsal heads, Charcot joint). Autonomic neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin. Peripheral arterial disease and poor healing then allow minor skin breaks to enlarge and become infected. Foot osteomyelitis is almost always acquired by the exogenous (contiguous) route, progressing from skin/soft-tissue infection into bone, and can also follow deep wound infection after foot surgery (p.1111, 3271).
additionalDifferentials: Charcot neuroarthropathy (neuropathic joint disease) — can mimic or coexist with foot osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272)
nonInfectiousMimics: Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy with bony deformity, which can radiographically and clinically resemble osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272)
Callus or pressure changes from abnormal foot biomechanics (p.3271)
additionalInvestigations: Probe-to-bone test with a blunt sterile instrument as a bedside clinical assessment (p.92, 1112, 3272)
Bone biopsy with culture (preferred basis for diagnosing/treating osteomyelitis given poor swab-to-bone correlation) (p.1112)
Cultures taken from the debrided ulcer base, purulent drainage, or wound aspiration rather than superficial swabs (p.3272)
MRI when pretest probability is lower or imaging needed (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 80-90%) (p.1112)
Nuclear medicine studies (PET, CT/SPECT) or labeled white-cell scans as alternatives to MRI (p.3272)
Ankle-brachial index screening for peripheral arterial disease in diabetics >50 years with risk factors (p.3272)
redFlags: Wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) (p.1112, 3272)
Chronic ulcer failing to respond to therapy (prompt plain radiographs to assess for osteomyelitis) (p.3272)
Underlying peripheral arterial insufficiency / ischemic limb (contributes to non-healing and amputation risk) (p.3272)
Charcot foot deformity complicated by chronic osteomyelitis (p.1111)
harrison.prognosis: Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation. Diabetic foot osteomyelitis increases amputation risk; a foot ulcer (or subsequent ulceration) carries a 14-24% risk of eventual amputation. Adequate management of early-stage infection lowers the amputation rate, and wound debridement combined with antibiotics makes amputation unnecessary in roughly two-thirds of patients (p.1111-1112, 3271).
pitfalls: Do NOT rely on superficial swab cultures to guide therapy — they grow contaminants/colonizers and correlate poorly with bone culture (p.1112, 3272).
Plain x-rays have limited sensitivity (30-90%) for diabetic foot osteomyelitis and are mainly useful for follow-up of confirmed cases, not for early diagnosis (p.1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test does not fully exclude osteomyelitis, especially when pretest probability is low — pursue MRI (p.1112).
Antiseptic agents should be avoided and topical antibiotics are of limited value in wound care (p.3272).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison references the IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections but does not reproduce the detailed IDSA/IWGDF grading scale in this text. Infections are described broadly as mild/non-limb-threatening versus more severe (p.1112, 3272).
